title: Ang 990–1000: Nanak and Amar Das in Maru
tomorrow: why do the rich house and the poor house both lie awake?

cards: A busy register, a line out the door. The cashier takes a twenty, holds it up to the light, and swipes a little pen across it. Nobody's offended; that's just how you check.
Paper can be printed to look like anything. What counts is what's actually in it. On ang 990 Guru Nanak runs that same test, only not on money.
On a person. He starts with a picture: the body is paper, and the mind is the writing on it.

teach.h: THE BODY IS PAPER, THE MIND THE WRITING.
teach.b: The hymn, in paraphrase: the body is the paper, the mind is what's written there, and the foolish one never reads the writing on their own forehead.
In the true court the writing gets read, and a counterfeit is no use to anyone. Then the coin.
If there's real silver in it, Nanak says, everyone calls it genuine. Look at where that puts the test. Not on the outside print.
Not on whatever other people scrawl across you. On what's actually in the metal. That's where brave faith starts in Maru, and it isn't loud.
It's trusting the writing within more than the graffiti from without, and letting the true court do the reading.

After Guru Nanak, these pages carry hymns by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, in the same raga, so the walk through Maru becomes one Guru answering another across the years. The test doesn't change between them.
A coin rings true or it doesn't. Courage here begins with letting yourself be weighed honestly, and refusing to be ruled by every mark someone else leaves on the paper.

how: Maru hymns of Guru Nanak and Guru Amar Das are sung in kirtan in raga Maru and read in order in a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: a rumor about you reaches your new coworkers before you do. by Guru Nanak's coin test, what matters most?
o: fixing your image fast, before the rumor sets.
what's actually in you, which the true court reads.
nothing at all; inside and outside are both just paper.
games.why: the hymn moves the test inside: a coin with real silver is called genuine, whatever is scrawled on the paper.

practice: Hold a coin, a ring, or any small piece of metal in your open palm. Feel its weight, not the picture stamped on it. For the rest of the sit, let the outside marks go and notice only the weight.

wordCard.voice: Ang 990. Where Guru Nanak's Maru hymn calls the body paper and the mind its writing, and tests the coin for silver.
